blocks.markdown: **Syllabus source note.** The syllabus points to Rule 2 of the Philippine Copyright Safeguards and Regulations for a definition. That is an implementing-rule source rather than a numbered Code provision. Section 172 defines protected subject matter; Section 177 enumerates economic rights. RA 10372 amendments are noted where relevant.

Literary and artistic works are original intellectual creations in the literary and artistic domain, protected from the moment of creation: books, pamphlets, articles and writings; periodicals and newspapers; lectures, sermons, addresses and dissertations for oral delivery; letters; dramatic, dramatico-musical and choreographic works; musical compositions with or without words; drawing, painting, architecture, sculpture, engraving, lithography and other art; original ornamental designs, models for manufacture and applied art; illustrations, maps, plans, sketches, charts and 3D works on geography, topography, architecture or science; scientific or technical drawings or plastic works; photographic works; audiovisual and cinematographic works; pictorial illustrations and advertisements; computer programs; and other literary, scholarly, scientific and artistic works. Protection attaches by the sole fact of creation, irrespective of mode or form of expression, content, quality or purpose — not on publication, quality, commercial purpose or registration.

Subject to Chapter VIII, economic rights are the exclusive right to carry out, authorize or prevent: (177.1) reproduction of the work or a substantial portion; (177.2) dramatization, translation, adaptation, abridgment, arrangement or other transformation; (177.3) first public distribution of the original and each copy by sale or other ownership transfer; (177.4) rental of specified audiovisual, sound-recording, computer-program, data-compilation or graphic musical works; (177.5) public display; (177.6) public performance; and (177.7) other communication to the public. Economic rights are exclusive but subject to statutory limitations; owning a physical copy is not copyright ownership.

Copyright originality is independent creation plus at least a minimal amount of creativity — it is not patent novelty. The Muller logo (simple angled lines forming an arrow plus a cursive word) was denied protection for lacking sufficient creative authorship in delineation or form. Muller is a U.S. comparative authority only.
Copyright vests automatically when the work is created, irrespective of mode or form of expression, content, quality or purpose. Deposit or notice is not a condition to its existence.

Protected derivative works: (a) dramatizations, translations, adaptations, abridgments, arrangements and other alterations of literary or artistic works; and (b) collections and compilations of data and materials original by selection, coordination or arrangement. They are protected as new works, but protection does not affect subsisting copyright in the employed originals nor imply any right to use them. The publisher holds only the right of reproduction of the typographical arrangement of the published edition, in addition to the author's publication right.

No protection extends to any idea, procedure, system, method or operation, concept, principle, discovery or mere data as such — even if expressed, explained, illustrated or embodied in a work — nor to day-to-day news and mere press-information items, nor to official legislative, administrative or legal texts and their official translations. Copyright protects expression, not the underlying idea, system, fact or official legal text.

No copyright subsists in any work of the Philippine Government, but prior approval of the creating agency or office is necessary for commercial exploitation, and royalties may be imposed. This does not apply to government-owned corporations, which have the exclusive right to register their works. The Government may receive and hold transferred copyrights.
The author is the natural person who created the work. The creator is ordinarily the author; ownership may follow special rules for employees, commissioned works, joint works and audiovisual works.

Ownership rules: (178.1) in original works, copyright belongs to the author; (178.2) joint authors co-own, with co-ownership rules absent agreement, and separately usable parts belonging to their authors; (178.3) employees own creations outside regular duties even using employer resources, while employers own creations resulting from regularly assigned duties unless otherwise agreed; (178.4) commissioned works belong to the commissioner, but copyright remains with the creator absent a written stipulation to the contrary; (178.5) audiovisual copyright belongs to the producer, scenario author, music composer, film director and author of the adapted work, subject to the producer's statutory exercise rights and contrary stipulations; (178.6) letters belong to the writer subject to Civil Code Article 723. The commissioned-work rule is often tested: the commissioner owns the work, but copyright stays with the creator unless a written stipulation says otherwise.

Publishers are deemed to represent the authors of articles and writings they publish unless the contrary is shown, and may sue for infringement to protect them. Anonymous and pseudonymous works are protected for fifty years from first lawful publication — or, if the author's identity is revealed or no longer in doubt before expiry, Section 213.1 applies.

Do not use one duration for all works — identify the category: (213.1) ordinary Sections 172–173 works, including posthumous works: life of the author plus 50 years; (213.2) joint authorship: life of the last surviving author plus 50 years; (213.3) anonymous or pseudonymous works: 50 years from first lawful publication (identity revealed brings Section 213.1; unpublished works 50 years from making); (213.4) applied art: 25 years from making; (213.5) photographic and audiovisual works: 50 years from publication, or from making if unpublished. Section 214: post-death or post-publication terms always begin on January 1 of the following year.

blocks.markdown: During subsistence of the copyright, the owner of the copyright or any exclusive right may — to complete National Library and Supreme Court Library records — register and deposit two complete copies or reproductions, personally or by registered mail, in the Directors' prescribed form; only law-field works go to the Supreme Court Library. Registration and deposit are not a condition of protection.

Each published or for-sale copy may bear a notice with the copyright owner's name and the year of first publication — plus the year of death in copies produced after the creator's death. Notice identifies owner and year; it does not create copyright.

Section 180: copyright may be assigned or licensed in whole or in part; inter vivos assignment or license must be indicated in writing; exclusive economic rights may be exclusively licensed, with the licensee receiving the rights and remedies within scope and the owner entitled to regular statements of account. Section 181: copyright is distinct from property in the material object — transferring one does not transfer the other. Section 182: the owner may transfer or assign copyright or any part under the Act. Section 183: owners or heirs may designate a collective-management society, which needs IPO accreditation to enforce member rights. Always distinguish the physical copy from the copyright.
Limitations, fair use and first sale: Sections 184–188

Non-infringing acts: (a) private free recitation or performance of lawfully accessible works, or qualifying charitable or religious use; (b) fair-use-compatible quotations justified by purpose, with source and author; (c) media reproduction or communication of public lectures and current-topic materials for information where not expressly reserved; (d) current-events reporting to the necessary extent; (e) fair-use-compatible teaching illustration with source and author; (f) specified educational broadcast recordings, subject to deletion and film limits; (g) broadcasters' ephemeral recordings with their own facilities for their own broadcast; (h) qualifying government, National Library and educational/scientific/professional uses in the public interest compatible with fair use; (i) specified nonprofit performances without admission fees; (j) specified public display of published or transferred originals or copies; (k) judicial proceedings or legal-advice use; and (l) nonprofit specialized-format reproduction for blind, visually- and reading-impaired persons with required owner and date information. Each exception is conditional; the section must not conflict with normal exploitation or unreasonably prejudice legitimate interests. It is not an unlimited education or nonprofit exception.

Fair use for criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching including limited classroom copies, scholarship, research and similar purposes is not infringement; qualifying decompilation for interoperability may also be fair use. The four factors: (a) purpose and character, including commercial vs nonprofit educational purpose; (b) nature of the work; (c) amount and substantiality of the portion used; and (d) effect on the potential market or value. Unpublished status alone does not bar fair use if all factors are weighed. Teaching is not a blanket defense — RA 10372 added “limited number of copies for classroom use,” and the factors are considered together.

**Platform guidance is not statute.** The reviewer's cited YouTube Fair Use policy describes U.S. law and platform practice — it is not Philippine statutory authority. Decide fair use under Section 185's four factors.

Sections 184 and 186 do not impair the Government's right to make or authorize a translation or adaptation of a work, or publish it, when necessary in performing its functions. Determine the legal basis and scope of the government use.

A natural person may privately reproduce a published work in a single copy exclusively for research and private study. Excluded: (a) architectural works in building form; (b) an entire book or substantial part, or graphic musical works, by reprographic means; (c) data compilations; (d) computer programs except under Section 189; and (e) reproduction unreasonably conflicting with normal exploitation or prejudicing legitimate interests. The exception is narrow: one person, one copy, private research or study.

A nonprofit library or archive may make a limited number of copies to fulfill its mandate — for fragile or rare works, isolated articles or brief portions for research or study, or preservation or replacement of a lost, destroyed or unusable copy unavailable from the publisher. It is not general permission for unlimited scanning or public distribution.

First sale doctrine: after the first authorized sale or ownership transfer of a particular copy by the copyright owner or authorized party, the lawful owner may generally dispose of that copy, subject to the Code. It does not transfer copyright or authorize reproduction. The syllabus lists it separately; read it with the distribution and importation provisions, including Section 190.
Enforcement and infringement: Sections 216–217, 221–224

A person infringes by: (a) directly committing infringement; (b) benefiting from another's infringing activity with notice and the right and ability to control it; or (c) knowingly inducing, causing or materially contributing to another's infringement. Remedies include injunction; actual damages, legal costs, expenses and profits; statutory damages in lieu of actual damages or profits subject to the statutory minimum and factors; increased damages in specified technological-measure and rights-management-information cases; and seizure or impounding of evidentiary articles. RA 10372 expressly addresses direct, vicarious and contributory theories — identify which applies and prove its elements; remedies are distinct from liability.

Infringement or aiding or abetting it is a crime: first offense, one to three years and P50,000–P150,000; second offense, three years and one day to six years and P150,000–P500,000; third and subsequent offenses, six years and one day to nine years and P500,000–P1,500,000. The maximum applies in specified cases involving circumvention of technological measures or unauthorized removal or alteration of rights-management information and related knowing distribution, broadcast or communication. Criminal liability is separate from civil remedies, and penalties escalate by offense number.

Points of attachment: Section 221 protects works of Philippine nationals or habitual residents, audiovisual works of Philippine-headquartered or resident producers, architecture erected here and art incorporated in Philippine structures, and works first published here (or published here within 30 days of foreign first publication) regardless of nationality or residence. Section 222 covers Philippine-national performers, performances here, performances fixed in protected recordings, and unfixed performances in qualifying broadcasts. Section 223 covers recordings of Philippine-national producers and recordings first published here. Section 224 covers broadcasts of Philippine-headquartered organizations and broadcasts from transmitters here.
Related rights: moral rights and neighboring rights

Independently of economic rights, assignment or license, the author may: (193.1) require authorship attribution and name indication as far as practicable; (193.2) alter before publication or withhold from publication; (193.3) object to distortion, mutilation, modification or derogatory action prejudicial to honor or reputation; and (193.4) restrain use of the author's name with a non-authored or distorted work. Moral rights protect the author's personal link with the work, separately from economic exploitation.

Section 194: an author cannot be compelled to create or publish, but may owe damages for breach. Section 195: moral rights may be waived in writing, but no waiver permits false attribution or prejudicial name use. Section 196: attribution in collective works is deemed waived unless expressly reserved. Section 197: necessary editing, arranging or adaptation for publication, broadcast, film, dramatization or adaptation is not a violation absent contrary stipulation. Section 198: the Section 193.1 attribution right lasts during life and in perpetuity after death; the 193.2–193.4 rights are coterminous with economic rights. Moral rights are not assignable or licensable.

Performers hold exclusive rights to authorize broadcasting or communication of live performances, fixation of unfixed performances, reproduction, distribution, rental and making available of fixed performances, plus moral rights to identification and objection to prejudicial distortion. Performers' rights are neighboring rights, separate from copyright in the underlying composition or script.

Sound-recording producers hold exclusive rights to authorize direct or indirect reproduction, first public distribution, commercial rental, and making available from an individually chosen place and time, with related remuneration provisions. These protect the recording, not necessarily the underlying music or lyrics.

Broadcasting organizations hold the exclusive right to carry out, authorize or prevent: (a) rebroadcasting; (b) recording of broadcasts for communication of television broadcasts to the public; and (c) use of such records for fresh transmissions or fresh recording. Broadcast rights concern the signal or transmission, not automatically every underlying work.
Chapter VIII's copyright limitations apply mutatis mutandis to performers, sound-recording producers and broadcasting organizations.

Where a section is condensed, the extract is a navigation aid only; verify and memorize full wording from the linked primary sources (RA 10173, RA 8293, RA 10372, NPC, IPOPHL).
